mathcounts-sample-school-team-02.title: Inclusion–exclusion
mathcounts-sample-school-team-02.body:
The forbidden neighbors are $\{1,4\}$ and $\{2,3\}$. Of the $4! = 24$ arrangements, those with 1 and 4 adjacent: treat them as a block, $3! \cdot 2 = 12$. Likewise 12 with 2 and 3 adjacent. Both blocks: $2! \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 8$. Bad: $12 + 12 - 8 = 16$, good: $24 - 16 = 8$.

**Answer: 8 ways**

mathcounts-sample-school-team-02.title: Build directly
mathcounts-sample-school-team-02.body:
Start with 1: its neighbor can’t be 4, so the next is 2 or 3. 1-2-?: next can’t be 3, so 4, then 3: 1243. 1-3-?: next can’t be 2, so 4, then 2: 1342. So 2 arrangements start with 1; by symmetry 2 start with each digit: $4 \times 2 = 8$.

**Answer: 8 ways**

mathcounts-sample-school-team-03.title: Count the group
mathcounts-sample-school-team-03.body:
In seventh grade, $\frac13$ of students don’t own a dog: $108 \div 3 = 36$. There are $93 + 108 = 201$ entrants, so the probability is $\frac{36}{201} = \frac{12}{67}$.

**Answer: $\frac{12}{67}$**

mathcounts-sample-school-team-04.title: Fill the grid
mathcounts-sample-school-team-04.body:
Each outlined pair is $\{1,4\}$ or $\{2,3\}$, so 5 never appears in a pair. Label cells (row, column) from the top left.

1. Row 5 has 3 in the corner, so its left pair is $\{1,4\}$; the remaining cells (5,3), (5,4) are 2 and 5. Cell (5,4) is in a pair, so it is 2 and (5,3) = 5; its partner (4,4) = 3.
2. Column 4 now has 3 and 2, so the pair (1,4)-(2,4) is $\{1,4\}$ and (3,4) = 5. Row 2 already has 1, so (2,4) = 4 and (1,4) = 1.
3. Row 2 then needs 2, 3, 5: the pair (2,2)-(2,3) is $\{2,3\}$ and (2,5) = 5. Column 3 has 2 at top, so (2,3) = 3, (2,2) = 2.
4. Column 5 has 1, 3, 5, so (1,5), (4,5) are 2, 4; row 1 has 2, so (1,5) = 4 and (4,5) = 2.
5. Row 3 has 5 and 1, so the pair (3,3)-(4,3) is (4, 1).
6. Column 1 has 1 in row 2, so (5,1) = 4 and (5,2) = 1. Row 1 needs 3 and 5 in (1,1), (1,2); row 4 needs 4 and 5 in (4,1), (4,2). Column 1 already has 4, so (4,1) = 5, which forces (1,1) = 3.

Corners: $3 \cdot 4 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 = 144$.

**Answer: 144**

mathcounts-sample-school-team-05.title: Orbit circumference
mathcounts-sample-school-team-05.body:
Increasing a circle’s radius by 400 km increases its circumference by $2\pi \cdot 400 \approx 2513.3$ km. The orbit is about $40{,}075 + 2513.3 = 42{,}588.3$ km long. Time: $\frac{42{,}588.3}{28{,}000} \approx 1.52101$ h $\times 60 \approx 91.3$ minutes.

**Answer: 91.3 minutes**

mathcounts-sample-school-team-05.title: Via the radius
mathcounts-sample-school-team-05.body:
Earth’s radius is $\frac{40{,}075}{2\pi} \approx 6378.1$ km, so the orbit radius is $\approx 6778.1$ km and its circumference $\approx 2\pi \cdot 6778.1 \approx 42{,}588$ km. At 28,000 km/h this takes $\approx 91.3$ minutes.

**Answer: 91.3 minutes**

mathcounts-sample-school-team-06.title: Count the complement
mathcounts-sample-school-team-06.body:
There are $3^3 = 27$ equally likely assignments. The best house is the one where the median child lives. They play at A exactly when at least two children live in A: all three in A (1 way) or exactly two ($3 \cdot 2 = 6$ ways), 7 in total. Likewise 7 for C. So house B is chosen in $27 - 14 = 13$ cases: probability $\frac{13}{27}$.

**Answer: $\frac{13}{27}$**

mathcounts-sample-school-team-06.title: Count directly
mathcounts-sample-school-team-06.body:
B is chosen when the median child is in B: either at least two children live in B ($1 + 3 \cdot 2 = 7$ ways), or exactly one lives in each house ($3! = 6$ ways). Total $13$ of 27.

**Answer: $\frac{13}{27}$**

mathcounts-sample-school-team-08.title: Base and height
mathcounts-sample-school-team-08.body:
Take $BC = 6$ as the base. The height is the distance from $E$ to line $BC$: the side of the square (6) plus the height of the equilateral triangle, $\frac{\sqrt3}{2} \cdot 6 = 3\sqrt3$. Area $= \frac12 \cdot 6 \cdot (6 + 3\sqrt3) = 18 + 9\sqrt3 \approx 33.6$ ft².

**Answer: 33.6 ft²**

mathcounts-sample-school-team-08.title: Coordinates
mathcounts-sample-school-team-08.body:
Put $A = (0,0)$, $D = (6,0)$, $B = (0,6)$, $C = (6,6)$, so $E = (3, -3\sqrt3)$. Triangle $BEC$ has a horizontal base of length 6 at $y = 6$ and apex at $y = -3\sqrt3$: area $\frac12 \cdot 6 \cdot (6 + 3\sqrt3) \approx 33.59$.

**Answer: 33.6 ft²**

mathcounts-sample-school-team-09.title: Enclosing rectangle
mathcounts-sample-school-team-09.body:
Box the quadrilateral in the rectangle $-3 \le x \le 7$, $-4 \le y \le 6$, area $10 \times 10 = 100$. Each vertex lies on a side of the rectangle, so the rest of the rectangle is four right triangles:
- top-left, between $A$ and $B$: legs 3 and 2, area 3
- top-right, between $B$ and $C$: legs 7 and 4, area 14
- bottom-right, between $C$ and $D$: legs 9 and 6, area 27
- bottom-left, between $D$ and $A$: legs 1 and 8, area 4

Area $= 100 - 3 - 14 - 27 - 4 = 52$.

**Answer: 52 units²**

mathcounts-sample-school-team-10.title: Complete blocks of 1010
mathcounts-sample-school-team-10.body:
Coprimality to 2020 depends only on $n \bmod 1010$, and each block of 1010 consecutive integers contains $\varphi(1010) = 1 \cdot 4 \cdot 100 = 400$ such numbers. $10^6 = 990 \cdot 1010 + 100$, giving $990 \cdot 400 = 396{,}000$, plus those among $1, \dots, 100$ coprime to 10 (101 doesn’t matter there): 40. Total $396{,}040$.

**Answer: 396,040 integers**
